stem: A 31-year-old develops ascending symmetrical leg weakness and areflexia following diarrhoea. FVC is 17 mL/kg; he cannot count beyond 10 in one breath.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate immediate step?
options: Urgent critical-care respiratory review, serial mechanics and assessment for IVIG
Wait for nerve-conduction testing before monitoring
explanations: Normal SpO₂ does not exclude neuromuscular ventilatory failure.
FVC below about 20 mL/kg raises concern for respiratory failure in GBS; involve critical care and consider IVIG or plasma exchange.
Steroids alone do not improve GBS outcomes.
Electrophysiology must not delay airway risk evaluation.
Physiotherapy does not replace acute treatment.
pearl: Serial FVC and bulbar function are key in Guillain–Barré syndrome.
pivot: Autonomic instability and poor cough further increase ICU risk.

stem: A 64-year-old has continuous severe vertigo, vomiting, truncal ataxia and direction-changing nystagmus. Head impulse testing by an experienced clinician is normal.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Investigate urgently for posterior circulation stroke
Reassure because no limb weakness is present
explanations: Continuous central signs are not typical BPPV.
Central HINTS findings and severe ataxia require a stroke assessment.
Vestibular neuritis usually has an abnormal head impulse.
No bacterial ear findings support antibiotics.
Brainstem or cerebellar infarction may lack limb weakness.
pearl: Central vertigo can occur without weakness or dysarthria.
pivot: HINTS is only valid in acute vestibular syndrome and with trained examiners.

stem: A 70-year-old has thunderclap headache and meningism. CT brain 12 hours later shows no haemorrhage; suspicion for subarachnoid haemorrhage remains high.
ask: What should happen next?
options: Discuss further investigation such as LP or CT angiography under local SAH pathway
explanations: CT sensitivity declines with time.
A negative CT after six hours does not safely exclude SAH in all cases; pursue local pathway testing.
EEG is not an SAH test.
Skull radiographs cannot exclude SAH.
Antiplatelet therapy before excluding bleeding can be harmful.
pearl: High suspicion persists despite a negative later CT.
pivot: A high-quality CT within six hours may be sufficient in selected neurologically intact patients.

stem: A 58-year-old with fatigable ptosis and diplopia now develops weak cough, dysphagia and shallow breathing.
ask: Which measurement best guides urgent ventilatory risk?
options: Serial FVC and negative inspiratory force with airway assessment
explanations: Visual acuity is not a breathing test.
Respiratory mechanics and bulbar function detect impending myasthenic crisis.
Oxygen saturation can remain normal until late.
Antibody titres do not predict acute respiratory status.
Bilirubin has no relevant role.
pearl: Myasthenic crisis is an airway and ventilation emergency.
pivot: If bulbar dysfunction increases, plan intubation early.

stem: A 42-year-old has headache, confusion, focal seizures and a temporal-lobe MRI lesion. HSV PCR is pending.
ask: Which intervention is MOST appropriate now?
options: Start IV aciclovir while investigating encephalitis
explanations: Treatment delay can worsen HSV encephalitis outcomes.
Temporal encephalitis warrants early IV aciclovir and supportive care.
Aspirin is not pathogen treatment.
Fluconazole does not treat HSV.
Confusion and seizures require admission.
pearl: Treat suspected HSV encephalitis before PCR confirmation.
pivot: Early negative PCR can occasionally warrant repeat testing if suspicion remains high.

stem: A 25-year-old with headache and papilloedema has obesity and takes doxycycline. Neurological examination reveals abducens nerve palsy.
ask: What investigation should precede LP?
options: MRI or CT brain with assessment of cerebral venous sinuses
explanations: EEG does not exclude venous sinus thrombosis.
Papilloedema demands imaging to exclude structural and venous causes before LP.
Foot imaging is unrelated.
Hearing tests do not assess ICP.
Biopsy is not indicated.
pearl: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension requires exclusion of secondary causes.
pivot: Headache with new focal deficit or impaired consciousness raises urgency for structural investigation.

stem: A 34-year-old develops bilateral leg weakness, urinary retention and numbness below the umbilicus over 24 hours.
ask: What is the MOST important next test?
options: Outpatient nerve studies in six weeks
Urgent MRI spine and neurological or spinal surgical assessment
explanations: Peripheral testing risks delay.
A sensory level plus bladder dysfunction indicates spinal cord pathology.
Ankle films are irrelevant.
BP recording cannot exclude compression.
Abdominal CT is not adequate cord evaluation.
pearl: Bladder symptoms and sensory level are spinal red flags.
pivot: Back pain with fever adds concern for epidural abscess.

stem: A 30-year-old started lamotrigine three weeks ago and now has fever, skin pain, widespread blistering and oral mucosal erosions.
ask: Which response is MOST appropriate?
options: Stop culprit drug and arrange urgent inpatient assessment for SJS/TEN
explanations: Supportive emollients do not address severe drug reaction.
Mucosal lesions with epidermal injury demand urgent cessation and specialist care.
Higher exposure can worsen reaction.
Outpatient symptomatic management is unsafe.
Rechallenge risks recurrence or death.
pearl: Lamotrigine plus mucosal rash is an emergency.
pivot: Simple benign exanthem lacks mucosal detachment or systemic illness.

stem: A 62-year-old with lung cancer has new severe back pain, progressive leg weakness and urinary retention. Examination reveals a thoracic sensory level.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate initial pathway?
options: Emergency spinal MRI, immediate specialist referral and dexamethasone as indicated
explanations: Therapy alone delays diagnosis.
Metastatic spinal cord compression needs urgent imaging, steroids where appropriate and surgical or radiation evaluation.
Analgesia alone risks paralysis.
LP is not the first investigation and may be inappropriate.
Anticoagulation does not treat cord compression.
pearl: New bladder dysfunction with cancer and back pain is cord compression until proven otherwise.
pivot: Early intervention can preserve walking ability.

stem: A 48-year-old with thunderclap headache and new third nerve palsy has an enlarged, poorly reactive pupil.
ask: Which cause must be urgently excluded?
explanations: Tension headache cannot explain painful pupillary third-nerve dysfunction.
Compressive aneurysm can cause a painful pupil-involving third nerve palsy.
Migraine does not safely explain this focal finding.
Cataract does not impair eye movements.
CN VII palsy does not produce a third nerve palsy.
pearl: Painful third nerve palsy involving the pupil: urgent vascular imaging.
pivot: Microvascular third nerve palsy more often spares the pupil but still requires clinical evaluation.

stem: A 46-year-old given haloperidol develops severe lead-pipe rigidity, fever 40°C, autonomic instability and CK 6000 U/L over 48 hours.
ask: Which action is MOST appropriate?
options: Stop dopamine antagonist and provide urgent supportive management for NMS
explanations: Further blockade exacerbates NMS.
NMS requires drug cessation and critical supportive monitoring; adjunct medication may be considered.
Organic toxicity is clear.
SSRIs do not treat NMS.
Life-threatening complications need admission.
pearl: NMS: rigidity and CK elevation, often over days.
pivot: Clonus and hyperreflexia after serotonergic exposure instead favour serotonin syndrome.

stem: A mother has unwanted intrusive thoughts of stabbing her infant and avoids knives. She is distressed and has intact insight without hallucinations or intent.
ask: Which diagnosis BEST fits?
explanations: Psychosis implies compromised reality testing or psychotic symptoms not described.
Intrusive unwanted thoughts, avoidance and intact insight point toward OCD.
The patient recognises the thoughts as her own unwanted fears.
There is no antisocial pattern.
Manic activation is not described.
pearl: Ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts differ from psychotic intent.
pivot: Always assess safety; a delusional belief or plan would change urgency.

stem: A 26-year-old sleeps only two hours nightly yet feels energetic, speaks rapidly, spends thousands and has grandiose delusions. Occupational functioning is markedly impaired.
ask: Which is the MOST likely episode?
explanations: Hypomania does not include psychosis or marked impairment.
Mania can involve impaired function, grandiosity and psychosis.
Panic involves discrete attacks rather than sustained activated mood.
Anxiety does not explain grandiose delusions and reduced need for sleep.
Depression is inconsistent with activation.
pearl: Psychosis or marked impairment indicates mania rather than hypomania.
pivot: Always assess stimulant use, thyroid disease and medication triggers.

stem: A 79-year-old with pneumonia becomes confused overnight, alternating drowsiness with agitation; attention is impaired, though she lived independently last week.
ask: Which diagnosis BEST explains this?
explanations: Alzheimer disease progresses more gradually.
Acute fluctuation and inattention are hallmark delirium features.
Intellectual disability is developmental.
Schizophrenia does not typically cause fluctuating consciousness with infection.
Insomnia alone cannot explain profound inattention.
pearl: Check attention when distinguishing delirium from dementia.
pivot: Delirium may coexist with underlying dementia.

stem: A man who drinks a bottle of spirits daily stopped 48 hours ago. He is tremulous, hypertensive, diaphoretic and seeing insects; attention fluctuates.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Benzodiazepine-based withdrawal treatment with thiamine and medical monitoring
explanations: Antipsychotics do not prevent withdrawal seizures.
Severe alcohol withdrawal needs sedative-based protocol, thiamine and monitoring.
Disulfiram is relapse prevention, not emergency management.
Opioids compound sedation and harm.
Severe withdrawal can be fatal.
pearl: Delirium tremens is a medical emergency.
pivot: Treat concurrent Wernicke encephalopathy risk promptly.

stem: A woman on phenelzine develops severe headache, palpitations and BP 220/125 mmHg after aged cheese.
ask: Which mechanism BEST explains this?
options: Tyramine-related catecholamine excess during MAO inhibition
explanations: Insulin blockade is not the mechanism.
MAO inhibition prevents tyramine metabolism, precipitating hypertensive crisis.
Histamine changes do not explain this characteristic interaction.
Warfarin mechanism is unrelated.
Dopamine blockade does not explain tyramine toxicity.
pearl: MAOIs interact with tyramine-rich foods and sympathomimetics.
pivot: MAOI combined with an SSRI can instead provoke serotonin toxicity.

stem: A patient presents with superficial cutting and says it relieves tension, but sometimes she wishes she were dead. She now wants to leave.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate response?
options: Assess suicide intent, means, capacity and protective factors while treating injuries and planning safety
explanations: Nonsuicidal self-injury does not eliminate suicide risk.
Compassionate individualised risk assessment and treatment are essential.
Punishment reduces trust.
Safety duties can override confidentiality in limited circumstances.
Asking about plans improves assessment rather than causing suicidality.
pearl: Distinguish self-harm intent while acknowledging it can fluctuate.
pivot: Current intent with access to lethal means merits immediate protective action.

stem: A patient with schizophrenia remains psychotic after two adequately dosed, adhered-to antipsychotic trials with no substance use.
ask: Which option is MOST evidence-based next?
options: Offer clozapine with blood and other safety monitoring
explanations: Repeated ineffective treatment does not address resistance.
Clozapine is indicated for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and requires ANC and other monitoring.
Benzodiazepines are not antipsychotic maintenance.
Cessation risks relapse.
Antibiotics are irrelevant.
pearl: Clozapine is best established after two adequate failed trials.
pivot: Confirm adherence and adequate dose/duration before declaring resistance.

stem: A patient ingested a large amount of paracetamol five hours ago intending suicide, and now says she regrets it and wants discharge.
ask: What is the BEST approach?
options: Urgently evaluate ingestion timing, paracetamol concentration, antidote needs, capacity and suicide risk
Give activated charcoal regardless of timing and airway
explanations: Regret does not remove medical risk.
The time-sensitive toxicology pathway and psychiatric safety evaluation are both needed.
Delay can miss N-acetylcysteine window.
Charcoal is not routinely safe or useful at arbitrary late times.
Long-term treatment does not replace overdose care.
pearl: Patients may look well early in dangerous paracetamol toxicity.
pivot: Unknown timing or staggered ingestion requires a different assessment than a single acute nomogram.

stem: A 29-year-old has recurring unexpected panic attacks and now avoids exercise because palpitations might signal another attack.
ask: Which long-term treatment is MOST appropriate?
options: CBT with interoceptive exposure, with SSRI when indicated
Repeated CT scans at each attack
explanations: Long-term benzodiazepine monotherapy creates dependence concerns.
Exposure-based CBT directly addresses fear of physical sensations and avoidance.
Routine imaging does not treat panic disorder.
Antipsychotics are not first-line.
Avoidance strengthens feared associations.
pearl: Interoceptive exposure targets catastrophic interpretation of bodily sensations.
pivot: Triggered social fear rather than unexpected attacks suggests social anxiety disorder.
